verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Bhilwara dyeing and processing houses with captive power, verified effluent compliance and export order books; avoid job-work units with no captive power and thin receivables cover.
title: Bhilwara textile dyeing & processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
A dyeing and processing house takes grey fabric or yarn, wets it, dyes it, finishes it and returns it to a fabric maker or exporter. Cash comes in per metre processed, so the unit earns on throughput and yield, not on brand. **The two costs that decide survival are power and chemicals, and both are variable, so a unit with captive solar or a solid-fuel boiler holds margin when the grid tariff moves.** Bhilwara's cluster is investing more than Rs 3,000 crore across expansion [2], which tells you capacity is being added faster than local demand.

## Where value and cash sit now
Value sits in the order book and in the effluent treatment plant, not in the machines. **Working capital is driven by inventory holding and receivables [8], and the sector is fixed-capital as well as working-capital intensive, so funding needs are high [9].** The local signal is weak: Rajasthan GST collections are -4.7% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], and state electricity demand is +4.0% against India +9.5% [D]. Against that, India-wide IIP for NIC 13 output is +13.1% YoY [D]. Read this as a national textile pull with a Bhilwara-specific drag.

## What has changed
Two things. First, the 2026 waste rules require industrial units with solid-fuel boilers to divert non-recyclable textile waste into refuse-derived fuel, and garment factories and industrial parks must process wet waste on-site or buy compliance certificates [4]. **So when a proposal lands, check the boiler fuel and the waste contract; if the unit has no RDF tie-up or on-site processing, ask for the compliance certificate cost line and price it into the assessment.** Second, Bhilwara is exporting yarn and thread to Bangladesh to offset Middle East disruption [3], which widens the buyer base but adds country risk. Peer results are mixed: Arvind's Q2 FY27 net profit rose 44% to Rs 148 crore on revenue of Rs 2,919 crore, up 23% [6], while Sportking's operating margin jumped to 19% in Q1 FY27 from 12% [7] after a weak FY24-FY26. Note the Arvind and Sportking figures are peer benchmarks, not Bhilwara units.

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
Pursue processors with captive solar or a compliant boiler, a named export buyer, and at least one year of audited throughput. **Structure as a cash-flow term loan against verified processing invoices, with a monthly stock-and-receivables statement and a power-bill covenant; take the GST return, the electricity bill and the buyer-wise sales register every month.** Where a figure is missing, collect from customer.

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly GST return (monthly): two consecutive months of falling turnover -> freeze fresh disbursement and inspect stock. - Electricity bill (monthly): units consumed per metre rising -> ask for the boiler and solar log, reprice the limit. - Effluent and waste compliance (quarterly): lapsed consent or missing RDF certificate -> stop renewal until cured.
